From 04 - Diagnostic Pathway for Breast Mass (its benign-lesion table).

stem: Rank each pathology report term from least (1) to most (5) malignant.
answer:
The pairings:

TerminologyRank (1 least to 5 most malignant)
Atypia Present, Cannot exclude malignancy3
Suspicion for Malignancy4
Atypia Present, Favour Reactive2
Positive for malignancy5 - most malignant
Negative for malignancy1 - least malignant

From 06 - Communication of the Pathology Report. When a diagnosis is not clear-cut the pathologist writes a narrative report using a graded vocabulary of malignancy risk. The lecture's scale runs positive → suspicious → atypia (cannot exclude malignancy) → atypia (favour reactive) → negative; reversed for least-to-most:

  • 1 - negative for malignancy.
  • 2 - atypia present, favour reactive: abnormal cells, but the pathologist leans benign.
  • 3 - atypia present, cannot exclude malignancy: abnormal cells with malignancy left open.
  • 4 - suspicious for malignancy: probably cancer, short of certainty.
  • 5 - positive for malignancy.

The two atypia terms are the trap: favour reactive leans benign, cannot exclude does not.

Involved in cancer screening, symptom relief, counselling and referrals

answer:
The pairings:

StatementTeam member
Perform biopsies for cancer diagnosis and play a role in removal and cancer staging.General Surgeon
Involved in cancer screening, symptom relief, counselling and referralsPrimary Care Physician
Provide education, resources and support to help patients and families navigate the cancer journeySocial Worker
Helps relieve suffering and improve quality of life at any stage in a serious illnessPalliative care physician

From 03 - Cancer Genetics (its interprofessional management table).

  • General surgeon: diagnostic biopsy, removal and staging, lymph node dissection.
  • Primary care physician: screening, symptom relief, counselling and referrals - the lecture's wording almost exactly.
  • Social worker: counselling through education, resources and supports, and advocacy in navigating recovery.

The near-miss for the education-and-support statement is the Indigenous health navigator, who also counsels and advocates, but the lecture defines that role as navigating the health care system. The pathologist makes the diagnosis on the tissue but does not perform the biopsy or the removal.

stem: Identify each activity as either an Activity of Daily Living (ADL) or an Instrumental Activity of Daily Living (IADL).
answer:
The pairings:

ActivityADL or IADL
AmbulatingADL (activity of daily living)
CookingIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
DressingADL (activity of daily living)
EatingADL (activity of daily living)
FinancesIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
Hygiene (bathing)ADL (activity of daily living)
Medication managementIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
ShoppingIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
Social engagementIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
TelephoneIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
ToiletingADL (activity of daily living)
TransportationIADL (instrumental activity of daily living)
TransferringADL (activity of daily living)

From 04 - Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment.

  • Ambulating is the A of DEATH, a basic ADL: moving from one position to another (transfers) and walking independently. It is physical self-care, not a household task that needs planning.
  • Cooking is the F of SHAFT (Food preparation), an IADL: it needs planning, sequencing and safety judgment, not just the physical ability to feed oneself. Do not confuse it with eating, which is a basic ADL.
  • Dressing is the D of DEATH, a basic ADL: selecting appropriate clothing and putting it on.
  • Eating is the E of DEATH, a basic ADL: the ability to feed oneself. Preparing the food is a different task - cooking is an IADL.
  • Finances are the A of SHAFT (Accounting), an IADL: the ability to pay bills and manage money, a cognitively demanding task of running a household rather than self-care.
  • Hygiene is the H of DEATH, a basic ADL: bathing and grooming oneself and keeping up dental, nail and hair care.
  • Managing medications is the extra M the SHAFT note adds to the IADLs: obtaining medications and taking them as prescribed. It depends on memory and organization rather than physical self-care.
  • Shopping is the S of SHAFT, an IADL: acquiring food and clothing.
  • Social engagement is not one of the named SHAFT items, but it belongs on the IADL side by the same logic: it is a higher-order activity of living in the community, not basic self-care of the body - and none of the DEATH items (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene) covers it.
  • Using the telephone is a T of SHAFT, an IADL, along with mail, internet and email.
  • Toileting is the T of DEATH, a basic ADL: getting to and from the toilet, using it appropriately and cleaning oneself, plus continence - control of bladder and bowel.
  • Transportation is a T of SHAFT, an IADL: driving or using public transport.

The split to remember: ADLs = DEATH (Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Hygiene), the basic self-care tasks; IADLs = SHAFT (Shopping, Housework, Accounting, Food preparation, Telephone/Transportation) plus managing medications, the household tasks that need more cognitive skill.

Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) can be remembered by the mnemonic DEAT(T)H: Dressing, Eating, Ambulating, Toileting, Transferring, Hygiene (Bathing). Instrumental ADLs are shopping, transportation, cooking, finances, telephone, medications, social engagement.

flags.title: Social engagement is not covered by the vault notes
flags.html:
No lecture note covers this; the reasoning is from general principles. Verify it before relying on it.

The vault's ADL and IADL lists (DEATH, SHAFT plus medications) do not name social engagement; the IADL classification follows the key and the logic of the split, not a lecture statement.

stem: Match each hemoglobin to its globin chain composition.

items.left: A tetramer molecule composed of 2 alpha and 2 beta globin chains.
A tetramer molecule composed of 2 alpha and 2 gamma globin chains.
A tetramer molecule composed of 2 alpha and 2 abnormal beta globin chains.

answer:
The pairings:

CompositionHemoglobin
A tetramer molecule composed of 2 alpha and 2 beta globin chains.Hemoglobin A
A tetramer molecule composed of 2 alpha and 2 gamma globin chains.Hemoglobin F
A tetramer molecule composed of 2 alpha and 2 abnormal beta globin chains.Hemoglobin S

From 01 - Hematopoiesis and 07 - Hemoglobinopathies. The pairing is HbF, 2 alpha + 2 gamma; HbS, 2 alpha + 2 abnormal beta; HbA, 2 alpha + 2 beta.

  • HbF (α2γ2) is the intrauterine hemoglobin. Gamma chains are replaced by beta chains in the first 3-6 months, leaving < 2% HbF in adults.
  • HbS has normal alpha chains with a mutant beta chain (position 6 Glu to Val). That is why sickle disease hides until about age 3, while HbF still protects.
  • HbA (α2β2) is about 95% of adult hemoglobin; HbA2 (α2δ2) is about 3%.

answer:

ImageStage
Image 1Stage 3
Image 2Stage 1
Image 3Stage 4
Image 4Stage 2

From 05 - Approach to Lymphoma. Ann Arbor staging depends on the number of regions involved and where they sit relative to the diaphragm (the dashed line in each figure).

  • Image 2 is stage 1 - a single node region.
  • Image 4 is stage 2 - three regions, all above the diaphragm.
  • Image 1 is stage 3 - nodes both above and below the diaphragm.

From 03 - Anatomy of a Mediastinal Mass. Sort by compartment boundaries: the anterior lies between sternum and pericardium, the middle is the pericardium and what it holds, the posterior is behind the heart against the spine.

  • Anterior: the internal thoracic artery and thymus (with nodes, connective tissue and fat: “I CAN'T”).
  • Posterior: the T3 vertebra (the spine is the posterior border, and posterior masses implicate spine and nerves) and the hemiazygos vein, with the esophagus, descending aorta, azygos system, thoracic duct and sympathetic trunk.
  • Middle: SVC, pericardium, phrenic nerve, pulmonary veins and heart, with the ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, IVC and recurrent laryngeal nerve.

stem: Match each disease to its targeted therapy.
answer:
The pairings:

DiseaseTargeted therapy
CLLBruton’s Kinase Inhibitor
CMLImatinib
AMLFlt3 inhibitor
APLATRA
GISTImatinib

From 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies.

  • Imatinib: CML, GIST. This tyrosine kinase inhibitor blocks the constitutively active BCR-ABL of the Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22), in CML, and is also used in GIST.
  • BTK inhibitor: CLL. Ibrutinib (and idelalisib) is used for CLL specifically. Its toxicities are bruising, atrial fibrillation and diarrhea.
  • FLT3 inhibitor: for AML.
  • ATRA: APL. It dissociates the PML-RARA block so promyelocytes mature in APL, and is given with chemotherapy to prevent a very high WBC count.

stem: Match each targeted therapy to its toxicity.
answer:
The pairings:

Targeted therapyToxicity
ImatinibDiarrhea
RituximabInfusion reactions
All trans retinoic acid (ATRA)Differentiation Syndrome
NivolumabColitis
IbrutinibBruising

From 07 - Pharmacology of Hematological Malignancies.

  • Imatinib: diarrhea, with muscle cramps, periorbital edema, cytopenias and effusions.
  • Rituximab: infusion reactions, the remaining pair once the others are placed.
  • ATRA: differentiation syndrome. ATRA drives all the leukemic promyelocytes to mature at once, which is why the lecture says it is given with chemotherapy to prevent a very high WBC count.
  • Nivolumab: colitis. PD-1 blockade releases immune toxicity: colitis, pneumonitis, rash, hepatitis, hypophysitis, nephritis. It is treated with steroids.
  • Ibrutinib: bruising, with atrial fibrillation. Ibrutinib also causes diarrhea, so bruising is the discriminating match.

stem: Match each type of infection to the specimen that you would collect.
answer:
The pairings:

InfectionSpecimen
UTIUrine
Infective arthritisSynovial fluid
Wound infectionTissue or deep wound swab
MeningitisCerebrospinal fluid

From 05 - Microbiology Lab. The specimen table follows one rule: sample the site of infection.

  • UTI → urine: suprapubic aspiration is the gold standard, then catheter or mid-stream. Never take it from a catheter bag.
  • Infective arthritis → synovial fluid: joints and other sterile sites need fluid or tissue.
  • Wound infection → tissue or deep wound swab: deep tissue beats a surface swab, which only grows colonisers. A biopsy of the advancing margin is best.
  • Meningitis → CSF: by lumbar puncture, 3–4 tubes.

stem: Match each effector with its corresponding role in thermoregulation.

items.right: They contribute to the internal production of heat via metabolism
They contribute to thermoregulation by facilitating the evaporation of water from the skin
They contribute to thermoregulation by producing heat via shivering
They contribute to heat loss by the exhalation of warm air
They contribute to thermoregulation by regulating the blood flow to the skin

answer:
The pairings:

EffectorRole in thermoregulation
Brown adipose tissue (BAT)They contribute to the internal production of heat via metabolism
Sweat glandsThey contribute to thermoregulation by facilitating the evaporation of water from the skin
Skeletal muscle cellsThey contribute to thermoregulation by producing heat via shivering
LungsThey contribute to heat loss by the exhalation of warm air
Cutaneous blood vesselsThey contribute to thermoregulation by regulating the blood flow to the skin

From 01 - Homeostatic Control of Body Temperature. Each effector in the note runs in one direction for heat production and the other for heat loss.

  • BAT: brown fat metabolism (driven by T3/T4) produces heat internally.
  • Sweat glands: cholinergic sweating cools by evaporation of water from the skin.
  • Skeletal muscle: contraction and shivering generate heat.
  • Lungs: airway evaporation and exhalation of warm air lose heat (dogs rely on panting).
  • Cutaneous vessels: sympathetic vasoconstriction shunts blood from the skin to conserve heat, and vasodilation increases skin blood flow to lose it.

From 05 - Microbiology Lab. The lecture's classification table sorts all six directly.

  • Gram-negative bacilli: Pseudomonas, E. coli, Proteus and Klebsiella all sit in the aerobic Gram-negative bacilli row — pink rods with an outer membrane and LPS.
  • Gram-positive cocci: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a staphylococcus (cocci in clusters) and Enterococcus sits with the streptococci (cocci in pairs/chains) — purple, thick peptidoglycan.

From 02 and 03 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely. The spectrum chart runs from penicillin (narrowest) to carbapenems (broadest).

  • Penicillin → focused: the lecture's example of a narrow-spectrum drug, covering GAS but not even S. aureus.
  • Cefazolin → focused: a 1st-generation cephalosporin (Gram-positive cocci, limited Gram-negatives), chosen in the cellulitis case precisely because it targets staph and strep, where ceftriaxone is “too broad”.
  • Amoxicillin → focused: an aminopenicillin; the lecture lists it as broad only in combination with clavulanic acid.
  • Meropenem → broad: carbapenems have the broadest spectrum of all and are reserved for serious or resistant infections.
  • Pip-tazo → broad: “wider coverage than we need”, since it reaches Gram-negatives, anaerobes and Pseudomonas.

stem:
Thermoregulation is the homeostatic balance between heat dissipation and heat production.

Categorize each term below as an effector, thermoreceptors, regulated variable, or feedforward system.

items.left: Primary sensory neurons in the skin, spinal cord, abdominal viscera, and brain

answer:
The pairings:

TermCategory
Body temperature at 37CRegulated variable
Primary sensory neurons in the skin, spinal cord, abdominal viscera, and brainThermoreceptors
Body temperature during hyperthermiaFeedforward system
Sweat glandsEffector

From 01 - Homeostatic Control of Body Temperature. The note frames thermoregulation as a negative-feedback loop: thermoreceptors → hypothalamus → effectors, holding the regulated variable at its set point.

  • Effector: sweat glands carry out heat loss.
  • Thermoreceptors: sensory neurons activated by warmth or cold, found in the skin, spinal cord, abdominal viscera and brain.
  • Regulated variable: core temperature held at about 37°C (normal 35.5-37.7°C).
  • Feedforward: body temperature during hyperthermia is left here by elimination. The note defines feedforward as the body acting in anticipation of a thermal change (e.g. responding to a cold breeze before core temperature drops).

From In-Class - Fever. The lecture classifies fever by onset: acute (< 7 days), subacute (1–2 weeks) and chronic/persistent (> 2 weeks).

stem: Match each antibiotic class to its site of action.
answer:
The pairings:

Antibiotic classSite of action
Beta-LactamsCell wall synthesis
MacrolidesProtein synthesis
QuinolonesNucleic acid synthesis
AminoglycosidesProtein synthesis
CarbapenemsCell wall synthesis
SulfonamidesFolate synthesis

From 02 - Choosing Antibiotics Wisely Lecture 1. The lecture groups antibiotics by the bacterial process they hit:

  • β-lactams → cell wall: bind penicillin-binding proteins and block peptidoglycan cross-linking.
  • Macrolides → protein synthesis: bind the 50S subunit.
  • Quinolones → nucleic acid synthesis: inhibit DNA gyrase, a type II topoisomerase.
  • Aminoglycosides → protein synthesis: bind 30S and cause mRNA misreading.
  • Carbapenems → cell wall: they are β-lactams, the broadest-spectrum ones.
  • Sulfonamides → folate synthesis: folate synthesis inhibitors (e.g. TMP-SMX).
